title: Every Decision Is a Prediction
author: Cristian Damian
summary: Cristian Damian argues that every leadership decision is an implicit prediction about what will happen as a result—but because leaders rarely make their predictions explicit, reality cannot correct their maps. Using a case study of a team reorganization, Damian shows how two people can observe identical outcomes for six months and reach opposite conclusions, because neither of them stated in advance what they expected to see change. The insight is structural: an outcome without a prior prediction is just a data point that gets absorbed into whatever story you already believed. Writing predictions down before acting is what transforms outcomes into feedback and makes reality's answers legible. The piece is a short, practical argument for treating management decisions as hypotheses that must be falsifiable to be useful.
points: Every decision is an implicit prediction—a claim about what will be different at a future date—but most leaders never articulate predictions explicitly, making feedback invisible.
Without a written prediction, an outcome is just noise that gets absorbed into the observer's prior belief; with a prediction, the same outcome becomes signal.
The piece illustrates how two people can honestly observe the same six months of evidence and reach opposite conclusions because neither said what they expected before the experiment began.
Reality 'answers' decisions constantly through events like missed handoffs, client complaints, and behavioral changes—but those answers require an explicit question (prediction) to be meaningful.
The practical fix is simple: state in writing what you expect to be different, and by when, before making a structural or personnel change.
quotes: Every map does two jobs. The first is explaining what you've already seen. The second is predicting what you haven't seen yet. People judge maps by the first. Reality judges them by the second.

You hire someone. Sitting across from them, you are making a claim: this person handles the work, and six months from now I'll be glad I picked them. That's a prediction with a date attached, and you almost certainly never say it out loud.
Reality answers, constantly, and faster than most people notice.
Without a prediction, an outcome is just something that happened. With a prediction, the same outcome becomes feedback.

That's how you and Dana can sit through identical months and walk out holding opposite conclusions, both of you honest. Neither of you was scoring anything, and impressions bend toward whatever you believed in January.
